title: Could you draw a familiar logo from memory?

sources.name: Blake, Nazarian & Castel (2015) — Original study abstract: memory and confidence for the Apple logo
UCLA — Report on the 2015 Apple-logo study and its undergraduate sample

practice: Try World Flags for another kind of visual question. Before choosing, notice which detail your answer depends on: a colour, a shape or its position.

sections.html:
Seeing a logo often does not guarantee that you can draw its details from memory. Familiarity and accurate recall are different things.

If you fancy trying a small example, choose a simple logo and keep it out of sight. Note how sure you are that you could draw it: not sure, fairly sure or very sure.

Sketch its main parts, or describe them in words. Then compare with the real logo. Ignore neatness; look for missing parts, extra parts and details facing the wrong way. Did it feel as easy as you expected?
sections.title: Familiar does not mean every detail is stored

sections.html:
In a 2015 study by Adam Blake, Meenely Nazarian and Alan Castel, participants tried to draw the Apple logo from memory and choose the correct design from similar versions.

Only one of 85 participants reproduced it correctly. Fewer than half picked the correct logo from the alternatives. Participants were more confident than their performance justified; overconfidence was lower when they judged their ability after drawing it.

UCLA’s report identifies the participants as undergraduates. This is a finding about that sample and task, not a percentage that describes everyone’s memory.
sections.title: A familiar apple surprised the researchers

sections.html:
Familiarity is the feeling that you have seen something before. Recall means bringing it to mind without the thing in front of you. Recognition means identifying something when it is shown to you.

Drawing a logo asks you to recall its parts and their positions. Choosing it from near-matches asks you to tell small differences apart. In the study, both tasks proved difficult.

The researchers suggested that people may not attend to details they do not need. Seeing a symbol often does not necessarily mean studying its exact shape. That is a possible explanation, rather than proof of one single cause.
sections.title: Knowing the look is not knowing every detail

sections.html:
Use your own sketch for this little comparison. You can describe the parts in words if drawing is awkward.

Three things to compare with the real logo
Look forAsk yourself
PartsDid I leave anything out or add something?
PositionDid I put each part in the right place?
DirectionDoes anything face the other way?

Circle one detail that surprised you. Then compare your first confidence judgement with what you actually drew. You do not need to turn the result into a score.

This is a small observation exercise, not a copy of the research test or a measure of intelligence. One sketch cannot tell you how good your memory is overall.
sections.title: Check one detail at a time

sections.html:
Before revealing a quiz answer, pause and name the detail you are relying on. “I remember the stripe order” is more specific than “that flag looks right”. Then check it.

If you want to practise a fact after checking it, follow our short routine for remembering quiz answers. If your first answer was wrong, see why the next explanation matters.

Does feeling very sure prove that every detail is right?

No. Confidence describes how sure you feel. Comparing your answer with a reliable reference checks whether its details are correct.
sections.title: Try the same pause with your next answer

description: A logo can feel familiar while its details stay fuzzy. Try a quick drawing challenge, then discover what an Apple-logo study found about confidence and memory.
